If you use an Apple Watch with gym equipment, GymKit should be on your radar. It's the best way to exchange workout data between Apple Watch and treadmills, ellipticals, and other fitness machines, producing measurements far more accurate than either could achieve on its own.

Apple launched GymKit back in 2017 alongside watchOS 4, but supported machines have always been hard to find. The good news is that nearly a decade later, you no longer have to spend around $15,000 to get a treadmill that supports GymKit.

These days, you can pick up a solid home treadmill with GymKit support for around $1,000. The BowFlex T6 treadmill is what I tested this summer, and with its combination of GymKit support, affordable pricing, and dial-based controls, it's an easy recommendation.

What makes Apple GymKit special

GymKit provides a two-way connection between Apple Watch and compatible treadmills, ellipticals, stair climbers, and indoor bikes.

Without GymKit, cardio machines can track your pace and distance, but need extra hardware to read your heart rate. Apple Watch can track heart rate, but has to estimate your treadmill distance and pace based on your arm movement.

GymKit lets the two devices fill in each other's gaps. Apple Watch sends heart rate data to the treadmill, and the treadmill sends back its own measurements taken directly from the workout.

According to Johnson Health Tech's director of product development Anthony Winge in an interview with 9to5Mac, calories, speed, distance, pace, time, incline, and heart rate sync in real time between the treadmill and Apple Watch, producing a more unified and accurate record in the Fitness app.

Using GymKit with the BowFlex T6

The pairing process is intentionally simple, but what surprised me was how flexible it is. You can connect Apple Watch before starting a workout, but you don't have to do it in that order.

For example, I could start a workout from the T6 console, get the belt moving, and then tap Apple Watch against the NFC sensor to confirm the connection. Being able to pair after starting felt like a small breakthrough to me. For some reason, starting from the treadmill and adding the Apple Watch afterwards felt more natural.

Once connected, Apple Watch offers four GymKit workout options: Indoor Walk, Indoor Run, Time to Walk, and Time to Run. The first two deliver the standard Apple Watch workout experience; the latter two let Apple Fitness+ subscribers combine the treadmill's GymKit data with Apple's audio-guided workouts.

Once paired, the treadmill and Apple Watch stay in sync. Pause, resume, or end the workout on either side, and the other follows along.

During your workout, your heart rate shows up on the treadmill console. As Winge noted, this is particularly useful for zone training, since you can monitor your heart rate without constantly glancing at your wrist or gripping the treadmill's metal sensors.

BowFlex has added GymKit across its current T6, T9, and T16 treadmill lines. In other words, this feature isn't reserved only for the most expensive model.

GymKit with iOS 27 on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3

Starting with iOS 27, GymKit no longer requires an Apple Watch. You can connect your iPhone to compatible equipment and use AirPods Pro 3 as the heart rate source. I tested this experience with the BowFlex T6, and it delivers essentially the same GymKit experience minus the watch.

Meanwhile, watchOS 27 has improved the accuracy of wrist-based distance estimates during indoor walk and run workouts. That helps when GymKit isn't available, but connecting directly to the treadmill remains the most accurate option.

Why GymKit has always been hard to find

GymKit's biggest problem has always been availability.

Initially, compatible machines only showed up at high-end gyms in major cities. The lineup has gradually expanded to more locations, including some Planet Fitness gyms, but support is still far from widespread. Even at a gym that has adopted it, you might only find the feature on a few machines.

Finding GymKit equipment for home use has been even harder. When I last looked in 2020, a Technogym treadmill compatible with GymKit cost around $14,000. That might be reasonable for a high-end commercial gym, but it's simply not an option for the average household.

At the time, I hoped that GymKit would eventually make its way onto treadmills in the $1,000 to $1,500 range. The BowFlex T6 sits exactly in that bracket.

BowFlex T6 brings GymKit back home

The BowFlex T6 treadmill is priced at $999 (originally $1,299).

For a fully featured home treadmill, that's still a reasonable price, coming in at roughly one-tenth of the GymKit models I saw last time.

The T6 also avoids expensive built-in touchscreens, opting instead for a straightforward console and an adjustable holder for your own iPad, tablet, or phone. That way you can choose your own workout platform rather than being locked into a single service.

You can use Apple Fitness+ (Apple One Premier), Peloton, Zwift, or BowFlex's optional JRNY platform. Your device can connect to the T6's built-in Bluetooth speakers, while the console continues to display the workout metrics you need.

The treadmill itself doesn't require a subscription. In an era when connected fitness equipment often requires an extra fee to access its best features, that distinction matters.

The dial controls are the most surprising highlight

Beyond GymKit and the affordable price, my favorite feature is how the BowFlex T6 handles speed and incline adjustments.

Instead of repeatedly tapping arrow buttons while walking or running, you turn dials built into the handlebars. The right dial adjusts speed; the left dial controls incline. I found this method faster and more intuitive.

BowFlex pairs these QuickDial controls with what it calls the MaxReact drive system, which responds quickly as you change speed or incline. For interval training that requires frequent intensity shifts, this control method is especially handy.

I first encountered this kind of dial a few years ago when testing Peloton's original treadmill. That machine was priced at a premium back then, so finding a similar control system on a much more affordable treadmill is a welcome surprise.

The T6 also includes a 20-by-60-inch cushioned running belt, a top speed of 12 mph, electric incline up to 15%, a three-speed fan, and a folding deck. These are solid fundamentals for a home treadmill, and they don't force you to pay extra for a giant touchscreen.

The bottom line

Overall, I strongly recommend the BowFlex T6 treadmill for anyone looking to build a home gym on a budget. BowFlex offers more expensive models with more advanced screens and larger running decks, but the T6 already delivers on the key features without adding costs I don't need.

Its GymKit experience with Apple Watch has been excellent, and it recently expanded to iPhone and AirPods Pro 3. If you want to use a Samsung Galaxy Watch, this treadmill supports that as well.

Have you used Apple Watch with Apple GymKit before? Share your experience in the comments.
